worksheet.title: Turning in Code
worksheet.subtitle: Ontario Math C3.1 — repeating events (move + turn)
worksheet.learning_goal: I can read a loop that makes Bit move and turn.

parts.title: Move, then turn
text: Last time Bit moved in a straight line. Now we add a turn inside the loop, so Bit moves AND turns each time around.
The turn amount is given to you (a square corner is right 90). Read the loop and see the path Bit draws.

parts.title: The same thing in Python
parts.output: Bit draws 3 sides with 3 right-angle turns.

parts.caption: range(3) draws 3 sides and 3 turns — one more side would close a square.

parts.title: Read it
parts.prompt: In the loop, how many times does Bit move forward? ______  How many times does Bit turn? ______

parts.title: Predict, then run
parts.prompt: You change range(3) to range(4) (forward 50, right 90 stay the same). PREDICT what shape Bit draws now. Then run it to check.

parts.title: Write your own
parts.prompt: Make Bit move and turn right 90, FOUR times. Fill in the numbers:  for step in range(______):  bit.forward(50)  bit.right(______)

parts.title: Challenge
parts.prompt: In  for step in range(4): bit.forward(50); bit.right(90) — Bit turns 90 each time. How many degrees does Bit turn in TOTAL? (Hint: it goes all the way around.)

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: Putting a move AND a turn inside the loop lets Bit draw shapes. The turn amount decides the corner; the number of repeats decides how many sides.

teacher_guide.eyebrow: Teacher Guide · Grade 3 · Intro Python Turtle
teacher_guide.title: Turning in Code
teacher_guide.subtitle: Quick facilitation notes & answer key

parts.title: Goal
parts.text: Students read a for-loop with a move AND a turn inside, and see that repeating move+turn draws a shape. Turn angles are given (no deriving). Sets up drawing a full square next sheet.

parts.title: Curriculum (Ontario Math 2020, Strand C3)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential, concurrent, and repeating events.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential, concurrent, and repeating events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.

parts.title: Materials
parts.text: Python Turtle projected (or a web playground); the printed worksheet + a pencil per student.

parts.title: Run it (about 30 min)
text: 1. Recall last sheet's forward-only loop; add a right(90) inside and run it.
2. Trace the range(3) path together — 3 sides, 3 turns, open.
3. Students do Exercises 1–4 (Ex 4 is the stretch), solo or in pairs.
4. Share answers; predict that range(4) closes the square (next sheet).

parts.title: Answer key (checked by the run-gate)
text: Ex 2 — a square (range(4) adds the 4th side and closes it).
Ex 4 (challenge) — 360° in total (4 × 90 = a full turn).

parts.title: Watch for & differentiate
text: Common slip: forgetting the turn also repeats — both lines inside run each time.
Support: have students trace with a finger, saying 'forward, turn' each repeat.
Extend: ask the total turning for range(3) at right 90 (270°).

parts.title: Success looks like
parts.text: The student counts the moves and turns (Ex 1), predicts range(4) closes a square (Ex 2), completes the loop (Ex 3), and adds the total turning (Ex 4).
